questions.f: In Leach and colleagues' 2009 surveys, handing out a written agenda at the start of the meeting was linked to higher perceived effectiveness, while one circulated beforehand showed no significant link.
questions.x: The benefit is tied to sending it ahead, partly because attendees then feel more involved. The links were small and correlational, so the agenda's design and use matter more than its existence.

questions.t: A candidate joins a video interview with her laptop flat on the desk, so the camera looks up at her face. That low angle is a common setup mistake; the camera belongs at eye level or slightly above.
questions.f: A candidate joins a video interview with her laptop flat on the desk, so the camera looks up at her face. That low angle is the recommended setup, since cameras below eye level are judged most positively.
questions.x: Coaches warn a camera looking up at you can make you seem arrogant, and raters judged a slightly high angle more positively. Propping the laptop on books fixes it.

questions.t: On a client video call, look into the lens when you make your main point or a request, and watch the client's face in the window under the lens while they respond.
questions.f: On a client video call, look into the lens for the whole call, including while the client responds, so you never seem to break eye contact.
questions.x: Constant lens-staring adds to video-call fatigue and stops you reading reactions. Reserving lens gaze for key moments gives the effect where it counts while letting you see how the message landed.

questions.t: Placing the other person's video right under your webcam works because people are far less sensitive to gaze slightly below their eyes than to gaze off to the side or above.
questions.f: Placing the other person's video right under your webcam works because people are far less sensitive to gaze off to the side than to gaze slightly below their eyes.
questions.x: Chen found people about ten times less sensitive to downward gaze, and viewers assume eye contact unless sure it's missing. Sideways glances, like reading a side monitor, are the ones they notice.

questions.t: A product manager's slide is headed "Customer churn" above a chart of monthly cancellations. In assertion-evidence terms, that headline is still a topic, not an assertion.
questions.f: A product manager's slide is headed "Customer churn" above a chart of monthly cancellations. In assertion-evidence terms, that headline is an assertion, because a chart supports it.
questions.x: An assertion headline states the point to accept, such as "Churn doubled among customers who never finished onboarding." A topic label leaves each listener to infer the conclusion while also listening.

questions.t: Replace a slide titled "Q3 delivery performance" with five bullets by one headed "Late deliveries doubled after July because Warehouse B lost its night shift," above the chart that shows it.
questions.f: Improve a slide titled "Q3 delivery performance" with five bullets by keeping the title and adding the night-shift cause as a sixth, bolded bullet at the bottom.
questions.x: The sentence headline carries the conclusion, so leaders who only glance still get the cause, and the chart proves it. Another bullet keeps the topic title and still makes the audience find the point.

questions.t: An independent 2023 study of engineering students found assertion-evidence slides lowered perceived cognitive load but did not improve understanding.
questions.f: An independent 2023 study of engineering students found assertion-evidence slides improved understanding but did not lower perceived cognitive load.
questions.x: It replicated the lighter-load result from the developers' own studies but not the comprehension gain. That is why the method is a promising default rather than a proven rule.

questions.t: Waiting for a client call to start, a consultant asks five quick questions in a row about the client's weekend, team and commute, sharing nothing about herself. That one-way questioning can feel guarded or intrusive.
questions.f: Waiting for a client call to start, a consultant asks five quick questions in a row about the client's weekend, team and commute, sharing nothing about herself. That is skilled small talk, since more questions always make people like you more.
questions.x: Questions help, especially follow-ups, but small talk should be reciprocal. After a question or two she should add a short, relevant fact about herself so it feels like a conversation, not an interview.

questions.t: Joining a video call early, recall something the colleague mentioned last time, ask one follow-up about it, share a small detail of your own, then bridge cleanly to the agenda.
questions.f: Joining a video call early, keep to a quick "Busy week?" and let the silence sit until the agenda starts, so you don't seem to be prying.
questions.x: A specific opener and a follow-up show you were listening, a bit of self-disclosure keeps it balanced, and the bridge ends it gracefully. The generic opener and silence miss the rapport the minutes could build.

questions.t: Methot and colleagues found daily small talk at work had a cost as well as benefits: it disrupted engagement with work, though people high in self-monitoring were less affected.
questions.f: Methot and colleagues found daily small talk at work had a cost as well as benefits: it disrupted engagement with work, though people low in self-monitoring were less affected.
questions.x: Small-talk days brought more positive emotion and helping, but the distraction reduced helping too, least so for high self-monitors. Keep chat brief when a colleague is mid-task.

questions.t: Applying Strunk's "omit needless words" to a status update means striking stock phrases like "the fact that" while keeping the dates, owners and figures the reader needs.
questions.f: Applying Strunk's "omit needless words" to a status update means cutting it to the fewest, shortest sentences possible, even if dates, owners and figures go.
questions.x: Strunk said the rule did not mean only short sentences or dropping detail; it means every word should do work, as in cutting "the question as to whether" to "whether."

questions.t: William Strunk Jr. first printed The Elements of Style privately in 1918, as a short text for his own English classes at Cornell.
questions.f: William Strunk Jr. first printed The Elements of Style in 1918 as a commercial handbook for office and business writers.
questions.x: It began as a 43-page classroom text with numbered rules instructors could cite when marking work; a commercial edition followed in 1920, and E. B. White's revision in 1959.

questions.t: Linguist Geoffrey Pullum granted that The Elements of Style counsels moderation on the passive, but argued most of the sentences it offers as passives are not passives at all.
questions.f: Linguist Geoffrey Pullum argued that The Elements of Style bans the passive outright, though he granted that its example passive sentences are correctly identified.
questions.x: Pullum's complaint was about grammatical analysis: in the Strunk and White edition, three of the four example passives aren't passives. The rule itself allows the passive when it's convenient or necessary.

questions.t: After mispronouncing a client's product name once during a pitch, a consultant replays it for days, sure everyone in the room remembers it. That is the spotlight effect.
questions.f: After mispronouncing a client's product name once during a pitch, a consultant replays it for days, sure everyone in the room remembers it. That is the illusion of transparency.
questions.x: She overestimates how much others noticed and will remember her slip, which is the spotlight effect. The illusion of transparency is about overestimating how well others can read your inner feelings.
